name: Lengthening over nail (LON)

lead: Lengthening over nail (LON) is a surgical route to added height: the leg bone is gradually lengthened, and a rod placed inside the bone carries the load so the external frame comes off earlier than in conventional frame-only lengthening.

The bone is cut and slowly distracted by an external fixator while an intramedullary nail sits in place; once the target length is reached the frame is removed and the nail is locked to hold the bone through consolidation. A randomised study of 31 limbs compared it with conventional Ilizarov lengthening, a 2012 study compared it with internal kinetic distraction and reported fewer complications with LON, and a 2020 systematic review covered outcomes of cosmetic stature lengthening.

paras: People who pursue it treat it as a major, planned surgery with a long recovery: a stretch of gradual lengthening, a period with the frame on, then consolidation and physiotherapy before returning fully to normal activity. It is discussed alongside fully internal motorised nails as one of the cosmetic height options, and the shorter frame time is the main reason people choose it.

Reported complications include pin-site infection, delayed bone healing, and demanding rehabilitation. One study found that reamed nailing can adversely affect bone regeneration during distraction. It is a major elective surgery, and regulation of cosmetic lengthening varies by country.

chain: Bone lengthened with nail and fixator
Added height, faster return to normal life
angle.text: LON adds measurable centimetres of height by lengthening the leg bone with an external frame while a nail inside the bone does the load-bearing, so the frame comes off sooner. It has been reported in both cosmetic and non-cosmetic surgical series.

lead: Lengthening over nail (LON) is a limb-lengthening technique in which an intramedullary nail is placed in the bone and an external fixator is used for distraction, after which the fixator is removed while the nail remains [1][2]. It was developed to minimise the time patients wear a frame during femur lengthening [1].

For height, the appeal is a permanent gain in leg length, and therefore overall stature, from surgically lengthening the femur or tibia. A systematic review of cosmetic stature lengthening reported a mean gain of 6.7 cm across 795 patients, and the Vietnamese bilateral tibial series reported an average of about 7 cm in men and 6.5 cm in women.[3][4] Compared with classic Ilizarov frames, the nail carries load during healing, so the frame can come off earlier and the bone is protected from deformity and refracture after frame removal.[5]

A prospective randomised study of 31 limbs compared LON with conventional Ilizarov lengthening on length gain, external fixation index, consolidation index and complications [2]. A 2012 study compared LON with intramedullary skeletal kinetic distraction in femoral lengthening and reported fewer complications with LON [1]. Series have reported results of cosmetic lower limb LON [6][4].
infobox: Reported in case series and a systematic review
About 1 mm per day after a latency of about a week (Wikipedia)[8]

paras: LON was developed to reduce or eliminate frame time during femur lengthening compared with conventional ring-fixator lengthening [1]. Magnetic internal lengthening nails are a related approach that avoids external devices [7]. Reference sources on distraction osteogenesis describe motorised internal nails as an alternative to external devices [8].

Wikipedia's limb-lengthening article describes distraction osteogenesis generally: a latency period of about seven days before the device is activated, distraction at roughly 1 mm per day, a consolidation phase while the bone heals, and removal of hardware in a second operation.[8] With LON the nail remains in the bone and the frame is removed earlier than in frame-only treatment.[1][5]

Wikipedia dates the first proposal of the principle to Bernhard von Langenbeck in 1869 and the first clinical series to Alessandro Codivilla in 1905, whose high complication rates meant the method was not adopted; Gavriil Ilizarov then developed external fixation and distraction rates through studies from the 1950s onward.[8] LON emerged as a hybrid of the Ilizarov frame and intramedullary nailing, intended to shorten frame time, and was compared with internal lengthening nails as those devices developed.[1][7]

In a prospective randomised study of 31 limbs in 28 patients, 15 were lengthened over a nail and 16 conventionally, and the groups were compared on fixation index, consolidation index and complications [2]. A study comparing LON with intramedullary skeletal kinetic distraction found fewer complications with LON [1]. Bilateral tibial LON has been reported with complications and psychological outcomes in a Vietnamese series [4], and results of cosmetic lower limb LON have been published [6]. A study of tibial lengthening found that reamed intramedullary nailing had an adverse effect on bone regeneration during distraction [5]. A 2020 systematic review covers cosmetic stature lengthening outcomes and complications [3]. Related studies include biological enhancement of bone healing in tibial distraction with bone marrow concentrate and platelet-rich plasma [9].

Registered studies include LON pain beliefs and functional performance after cosmetic lengthening (not yet recruiting) [10], postoperative physiotherapy after cosmetic femoral lengthening [11] and video-feedback rehabilitation after bilateral femoral lengthening [12].

A study of tibial lengthening asked whether valgus deviation increases with LON,[13] and a 2012 study of limb lengthening over plate described an alternative to nails that avoids the infection risk linked with nails.[14] A technical note on lengthening over an existing nail covers post-traumatic femoral shortening rather than cosmetic cases.[15]

A 2020 systematic review of cosmetic stature lengthening included 11 studies with 795 patients; the main techniques were classic ring Ilizarov fixators (267 patients, 33.6 percent) and LON (253 patients, 31.8 percent), with implantable lengthening nails used in 63 patients. Mean lengthening was 6.7 cm (range 1.5 to 13.0) with mean follow-up of 4.9 years, and the authors reported averages of 0.78 problems, 0.94 obstacles and 0.15 complications per patient; ankle equinus deformity was the most common problem or obstacle.[3]

A retrospective study of 32 patients with constitutional short stature (24 men, 8 women) reviewed patient selection, bone and soft-tissue complications and functional and subjective outcomes after cosmetic LON.[6] In a Vietnamese series of 104 people undergoing bilateral tibial LON with SIGN nails, tibial lengthening was about 24 percent of pre-operative tibial length in men and 21.5 percent in women; outcomes were rated excellent in 81.7 percent and good in 18.3 percent, all patients reported improved self-esteem and quality of life, and equinus contracture, pin tract infection and valgus deviation were the most common complications.[4]

Reference sources note that cosmetic stature lengthening is unregulated in some countries, that infection, additional surgeries and shorter-than-expected gains have been reported, and that China's health ministry banned limb lengthening in 2006 after serious side effects [8].

Wikipedia reports that in India cosmetic lengthening is unregulated, that people as young as 13 or 14 have had the procedure, and that some patients developed infections and needed further surgery to walk or gained less height than expected.[8] Equinus contracture, pin tract infection and valgus deviation are the complications most often named in LON series, and a study of tibial lengthening reported that reamed nailing can adversely affect bone regeneration during distraction.[5][4]

timeline.event: Bernhard von Langenbeck proposes surgical bone lengthening (per Wikipedia).[8]
Alessandro Codivilla publishes the first clinical series, with high complication rates.[8]
